question: Regulation (EU) 549/2013, which establishes a European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010), requires all economic activities to be registered, including illicit activities (Section 1.79). However, only some of these activities are listed, reflecting a degree of arbitrariness.

The regulation’s uniform application via the NACE nomenclature has led statistics bodies in some countries, such as Spain, to include ‘offering or providing sexual services’. This inclusion could legitimise prostitution, despite the fact that Section 1.
79 requires economic activities to be by ‘mutual agreement’, which is difficult to establish in an environment that is closely tied to a lack of opportunities, exploitation and people trafficking.

This harmonisation of statistics appears to adopt a regulationist view of prostitution that is not dominant in the majority of Member States and does not have Parliament’s support, as indicated by the Noichl Report (2023) on the regulation of prostitution in the EU. In light of the above: 1.
What incentives is the Commission planning to put in place to correct this contradiction between the harmonisation of statistics and national diversity?
What mechanisms exist to establish whether these activities are voluntary and to avoid legitimising transactions connected to sexual exploitation?
Or, on the contrary, will prostituted women, pimps and traffickers be included in the population in employment?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2025) The European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010) requires that all economic activities are recorded, provided that all units involved enter the actions by mutual agreement. This obligation also covers some illegal activities.

The Handbook on the compilation of statistics on illegal economic activities in national accounts and balance of payments1 provides a common definition of illegal economic activities and guidance for collecting and compiling the related statistics in a consistent and coordinated way. The Handbook is explicit: ‘prostitution services that do not have the characteristics of an economic transaction, i.e.

those not based on mutual agreement; must be excluded from the measurement’ (§3.4, p. 33). Trafficking, coercion and exploitation are thus not reflected in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and other macroeconomic statistics. National authorities use information from law enforcement, health services and specialised organisations to ensure this distinction. The same principle applies to employment.

Only people who voluntarily provide services are treated as employed for statistical purposes. Neither traffickers nor persons forced into prostitution are counted as employed in macroeconomic statistics. Including certain illegal activities in macroeconomic statistics is a technical requirement to ensure that GDP and other figures are consistent and comparable.
The regulation of prostitution is a competence of the Member States.
1 As the Handbook on the compilation of statistics on illegal economic activities (Eurostat/ECB, 2018) further
